title: Variable-Length Positional Arguments
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of variable-length positional arguments in a Ruby program and name the key rule involved.
Apply variable-length positional arguments in a small example and predict its result before running it.
Identify one boundary or failure case related to forwarding positional arguments and verify the intended behavior.

content.intro: Learn Variable-Length Positional Arguments through a visual model, a minimal Ruby example, and a practical check.
content.why_it_matters: Understanding variable-length positional arguments helps you write code that is easier to explain, test, and maintain. It also helps separate Ruby language guarantees from runtime assumptions, dependency behavior, and application-specific rules.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Variable-Length Positional Arguments helps you reason about the *args pattern. In Ruby, prefer a small example whose inputs and expected result are easy to explain. This lesson connects the syllabus topic to practical code and highlights where assumptions or edge cases matter.

content_blocks.title: How to think about it
content_blocks.text: Begin by identifying the key rule: The *args pattern. Then connect it to Collecting extra arguments. The remaining syllabus points—Forwarding positional arguments—are useful checks before applying this in a larger project.

content_blocks.title: Example: Variable-Length Positional Arguments
content_blocks.code:
def greet(name = "learner")
  "Hello, #{name}!"
end
puts greet
puts greet("Mina")

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Run the example as written, compare it with the expected result, and explain why each line supports variable-length positional arguments. Next change one input or condition and predict the result before running it.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Create a second example for variable-length positional arguments using a different input. Add one edge case from the syllabus list (Forwarding positional arguments), state the expected behavior, and write a small test or manual check that would catch a regression.

content_blocks.title: Recap
